Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

foreign adjective

from or of another country

also foreigner, foreigners, from abroad, foreign country, foreign affairs, foreign words, foreign accent, exotic

classical

Cic. Off. 2.64: apud externōs populōs
Traupman 318: foreign (of another country)
Traupman 318

externus, externa, externum

adjective · Declension on Wiktionary

foreign: of another country, as against ours

What belongs to other states: foreign peoples, wars and affairs. Lewis & Short set it against domesticus and noster: rēbus externīs … īnstitūtīs domesticīs, in foreign and in home affairs (Cic. Phil. 2.69).

Other words

  • peregrīnus, peregrīna, peregrīnum — foreign: coming from abroad (people, goods, words); as a noun, a foreigner

    adjective · classical · Quint. 1.5.55: verba aut Latīna aut peregrīna sunt; Traupman 318: foreign (coming from abroad); foreigner; Traupman 318 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Traupman’s word for what comes from abroad, and his noun for a foreigner, peregrīnus, peregrīna. In Rome a peregrīnus was a free resident who was not a citizen.

  • aliēnigena, aliēnigenae m. — born abroad; a foreigner

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Nep. Eum. 7.1: sī potius ipse aliēnigena summī imperiī potīrētur · Declension on Wiktionary

    Very frequent in Cicero’s speeches; also used as an adjective (Lewis & Short).

  • exōticus, exōtica, exōticum — foreign, exotic (of goods)

    adjective · also used · classical · Plaut. Most. 42: unguenta exōtica; M-O s.v. foreign · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.; later Gell., Apul.)

    Ante- and post-classical (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens keeps it for foods and goods.

  • extrīnsecus — from outside, from abroad

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Ac. 2.48: objectā terribilī rē extrīnsecus (Lewis & Short); Traupman 267 · Wiktionary

    An adverb in classical Latin. Traupman gives it as an adjective, extrīnsecus, -a, -um, “from abroad”; Lewis & Short has the adjective only in late Latin (Tertullian), meaning “outer”.

Examples

  • verba aut Latīna aut peregrīna sunt. Peregrīna porrō ex omnibus prope dīxerim gentibus ut hominēs, ut īnstitūta etiam multa vēnērunt.

    Words are either Latin or foreign. And foreign words have come to us, I would almost say, from every nation, as people have, and many customs too.Quint. 1.5.55

  • quae in hortīs nāscuntur, alia peregrīnīs vocābulīs, ut Graecīs ōcimum, menta, rūta

    of the plants that grow in gardens, some have foreign names, Greek ones, like ocimum, menta, rutaVarr. LL 5.103

See also abroad, language, national, international.
